transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-05-12
Start: 16:00 PDT
Duration: 52 min
Attendees: Leah Martinez (Redwood AE), Connor Blake (Redwood SE), Amir Patel (CTO, Zenith), Sophie Nguyen (Head of Platform), Marco Ruiz (Sr SRE)

Summary (auto): initial reliability and incident-tolerance discovery. Customer evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private for payment workloads; main concerns multi-region failover, SLA expectations, and deterministic fallback policies to avoid outages.

[00:00] Leah Martinez: Hi everyone, thanks for making time today, um, quick intro — I'm Leah, AE on the Redwood platform, and Connor my SE will talk through the reliability and incident tolerance patterns.
[00:18] Amir Patel: Thanks Leah. We're evaluating Redwood for powering a couple of real-time payment flows, so reliability is like, top priority. We need plan for, uh, incident tolerance and predictable failovers.
[00:28] Connor Blake: Totally. Can you walk me through current stack — where inference lives now, are you self-hosting models, or using a cloud API?
[00:36] Sophie Nguyen: Right now it's mix — our fraud model runs on a mix of internal endpoints and a third-party API for embeddings; latency varies. For payments we need sub-200ms P95 if possible, otherwise fallback to a local heuristic.
[00:50] Marco Ruiz: And we have compliance constraints — logs retention, SSO, KMS for keys, and region restrictions for EU users.
[00:58] Leah Martinez: Understood. For payments, customers often ask about three things: 1) multi-region routing and automatic failover, 2) SLA and SLO alignment, 3) private deployment / VPC options for isolation. We'll cover all.
[01:12] Connor Blake: Quick background on options — Hosted (Redwood API) gives fast onboarding and global regions, Dedicated is reserved GPU pools with predictable throughput and isolation, Private deploys into your VPC/on-prem for max control. Each has different tradeoffs for failover and recovery.
[01:31] Amir Patel: For Hosted, how does automatic failover work if a region degrades? We can't have global outage during a model relic or KV cache eviction.
[01:40] Connor Blake: We do smart routing — policy-based. You can set priority by region, latency threshold, or error-rate. If primary region crosses SLO or certain error budgets, requests route to secondary region or to a fallback model variant. That routing is synchronous at our edge, so failover is quick, typically in seconds, but cold starts for a model in another region can add overhead.
[02:05] Marco Ruiz: Seconds is ok only if the overall user experience stays acceptable. Cold start adds like 300-400ms sometimes, that's a problem for sub-200ms requirement.
[02:16] Connor Blake: Right — which is why we recommend warm replicas in secondary region for critical flows, or lightweight fallback models that are always kept hot for instantaneous responses — tradeoff is cost.
[02:28] Sophie Nguyen: So that would be Dedicated or Private? Can Hosted keep warm replicas across regions?
[02:33] Leah Martinez: Hosted can — we offer cross-region warm replicas under Dedicated-like SLAs as an add-on; but Dedicated or Private gives you more control over reserved capacity for warm instances. For strict P95 targets at 200ms, most customers either use Dedicated reserved pools or a Private deployment so they can guarantee warm capacity.
[02:52] Amir Patel: Ok. What about graceful degradation — say the model becomes unavailable, do you have structured fallbacks? We want structured outputs to trigger downstream compensation flows.
[03:03] Connor Blake: Yes, you can define fallback policies at route level — fall back to a smaller model, a cached response, or a rule-based heuristic. Redwood's routing supports function/tool calling patterns so you can orchestrate fallback logic. There's also prefix/KV cache options to return cached completions for repeat or similar prompts.
[03:22] Marco Ruiz: I'm hearing KV cache, is that the key value cache for autoregressive contexts?
[03:26] Connor Blake: Yeah sorry, KV cache — sometimes transcribed as K V cache — it's our token-level cache to accelerate repeated context. It helps reduce cold-start costs because, uh, the effective context warms up faster.
[03:38] Amir Patel: Any examples of failover SLAs? Our procurement team asks for 99.9% across the stack, but I know model infra is tough.
[03:47] Leah Martinez: Our formal SLA depends on contract and tier. For Dedicated with reserved pools we can get to 99.9% availability for the serving layer; Hosted public API has a published SLA that's slightly lower unless you opt into dedicated-reserve. For Private, SLA is customer-managed but Redwood provides runbook, monitoring hooks, and an ops playbook.
[04:05] Sophie Nguyen: And how is routing evaluated? Is there health checks and circuit breaker thresholds?
[04:10] Connor Blake: Yes — active health checks, latency windows, error rate windows. You can set circuit-breaker thresholds and automatic fallback, and also manual overrides during incident.
[04:18] Marco Ruiz: What about consistency of model versions across regions? If we failover to a different variant, risk of behavior changes is high — especially in payments.
[04:27] Connor Blake: Good point. We have model version pinning and rollout policies. You can pin route to an exact model version and restrict cross-region routing to compatible variants. We also support canary rollouts and A/B at the model level to test behavior before promoting.
[04:41] Amir Patel: Does Redwood keep audit logs for routing/fallback decisions? For post-incident review we need the exact sequence of what happened.
[04:48] Leah Martinez: Yes, our Console keeps traces and decision logs — per-request metadata showing which route and fallback was used, timestamps, and error traces. We can retain per-route history as part of the enterprise package for audit windows you need.
[05:00] Sophie Nguyen: Encryption at rest/in transit — KMS or HSM integrations?
[05:04] Connor Blake: We integrate with customer KMS for Private, and for Dedicated we support bring-your-own-KMS. Hosted uses Redwood-managed encryption by default but you can opt into BYOK in enterprise agreements.
[05:16] Marco Ruiz: If we do a Dedicated pilot, how do we test failover realistically? We need to run controlled failover drills with synthetic traffic and damage control.
[05:25] Connor Blake: We recommend a 2-week pilot: one week functional and load tests in primary, second week run scheduled failovers to secondary and measure P95/P99, cold start penalties, and downstream effects. We'll provide a pilot runbook and load scripts.
[05:38] Amir Patel: For pricing — warm replicas across regions sounds expensive. How do you recommend we balance cost and reliability?
[05:44] Leah Martinez: Typical pattern: reserve minimum warm capacity for critical paths, route non-critical requests to cheaper or smaller models, and use prefix caching aggressively. Redwood Optimize can analyze traffic and recommend batching/quantization to reduce unit cost without affecting accuracy too much.
[06:00] Sophie Nguyen: Could you share a sample policy we might use? E.g., primary region up to 90% traffic, on latency > X route to secondary model variant with simpler architecture?
[06:09] Connor Blake: Yes — we can share example policies. For payments most customers use a threshold policy: if P95 latency exceeds 200ms for 30s window OR error rate > 1% then switch to fallback route. Fallback route could be smaller model or a cached response. We'll put that in the runbook.
[06:28] Marco Ruiz: What about multi-region data residency? EU lanes must stay in EU, but in failure maybe we still need to route within EU only.
[06:36] Leah Martinez: You can scope routing by geo — policy supports region restrictions so traffic for EU users stays within EU-approved regions and only fails over to other EU zones. If there's no EU backup, policy can route to downgraded local heuristics instead of crossing borders.
[06:52] Amir Patel: Good. Do you have customers running payments in production on Hosted or are they on Dedicated/Private?
[06:58] Leah Martinez: A mix. Many fintechs start on Hosted for speed and then move to Dedicated or Private as they hit scale and compliance. Larger payment providers often choose Dedicated for guaranteed capacity and isolation.
[07:10] Sophie Nguyen: Security team will ask about pen tests and SOC 2 — can we get your certs?
[07:14] Leah Martinez: Absolutely — I'll share SOC 2 Type II, ISO documentation, and our security whitepaper. Also we'll include the private deployment checklist for KMS and audit integration.
[07:25] Amir Patel: How do you instrument tracing? We need distributed traces to see where latency is accumulating — is that in Redwood or in our network?
[07:33] Connor Blake: We expose tracing hooks and headers; you can integrate with your tracing system. Per-request spans show queueing, model inference time, and network time. We also provide token-level latency breakdowns in Console.
[07:47] Marco Ruiz: A couple of edge cases — what happens if model behavior regresses after a rollout and we need immediate rollback?
[07:54] Connor Blake: Rollbacks are instant — routes can be pinned back to previous version, and automatic rollback policies can be set to revert if quality metrics degrade. We tie quality monitoring to prompt sets/evals so you can detect regressions programmatically.
[08:07] Sophie Nguyen: How granular are the SLOs you provide? We want per-route P95/P99 and per-token throughput.
[08:13] Leah Martinez: Console gives per-route and per-model dashboards including P50/P95/P99, tokens/sec, and cost. We can also export those metrics into your observability stack.
[08:23] Amir Patel: On contract SLA — you mentioned 99.9% for Dedicated. Is that just serving availability or does it include model correctness?
[08:31] Leah Martinez: SLA is for serving availability and latency targets; correctness is operationally measured via evals and quality alerts but not typically in an availability SLA. For critical use cases we support custom SLAs with penalties tied to regression detection — that's part of enterprise negotiation.
[08:48] Marco Ruiz: Can we run isolated network tests? Our security team likes to do a trial of VPC peering and test egress policies.
[08:54] Connor Blake: Yes — for Private and Dedicated we provide a network test harness and sample CloudFormation/Terraform scripts for VPC peering and routing. We'll include that in the materials.
[09:05] Sophie Nguyen: For the pilot, what data residency commitments do we have? We need to ensure logs for EU users stay in EU.
[09:11] Leah Martinez: We'll scope pilot to EU-hosted nodes for EU traffic and provide a data residency addendum. For Hosted we'll ensure region restrictions; for Dedicated we can assign pools in EU zones.
[09:23] Amir Patel: Anything we need from our side to get started?
[09:26] Leah Martinez: We'll need expected traffic patterns (QPS), latency targets, sample prompts, and a list of compliance needs. Also network contacts for VPC setup if you choose Dedicated/Private.
[09:37] Amir Patel: I'll get that to you. We'll also need a written pilot SLO doc so procurement can sign off.
[09:43] Leah Martinez: We'll draft that and send it along with SOC2/ISO.
[09:47] Connor Blake: I'll attach a sample fallback policy and runbook; also a checklist for warm replicas and cost estimates for having warm instances in two regions.
[09:58] Sophie Nguyen: One more quick question on monitoring frequency — how quickly can we detect a P95 spike and trigger failover?
[10:05] Connor Blake: Our detection windows can be configured down to 30s granularity with rolling windows, and alerts can trigger automated routing changes; you can also set manual approval gates for non-critical flows.
[10:16] Amir Patel: Good.
[10:18] Leah Martinez: Quick recap: next steps — Leah to send SOC2/ISO + architecture; Connor to send pilot runbook, fallback policy examples, and cost estimate for warm cross-region replicas; Zenith to share traffic numbers and compliance checklist. We'll propose a pilot start week of 2025-05-26. Does that sound right?
[10:38] Amir Patel: Yep, sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[10:41] Marco Ruiz: Thanks.
[10:42] Meeting end.

Notes: Some transcription artifacts present ("K V cache" spelled out in transcript, occasional speaker label slips). Shared artifacts referenced: drive link to pilot specs (drive.google.com/zenith/pilot-specs) and internal security packet (redwood.com/soc2.pdf).
